doc.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Fired on the Cape; four summers with Dave McKenna at The Columns
summary: Hackett's band was fired, and Warren Mannows hired Tate to work with Dave McKenna, learning tunes without calls or tempos.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well not gangsters but we were going to be there about five years and we lasted about five minutes. We all got fired. And the night we got fired, within a couple of months maybe, and Bobby had had his first major diabetic attack and it really set him back and he never really got well from it. This was in ’74 and he died in ’76 so he never really got over his first diabetic attack and it finally took him away. But the night we got fired a man named Warren Mannows, who has left us, he owned a place down the road on the Cape, this was down in I guess West Dennis, in a place called The Columns. It was West Dennis. And Dave McKenna was working there. And he asked me, he said, you know my ship had sunk. We were fired, I had a girlfriend living with me at the time, I had no money, and I had committed to a summer rental and she had left her job for the summer and taken a leave of absence and here we were on the Cape and about a week after we got settled in we were all fired. And the same night this man Warren Mannows asked me how would I feel about spending the rest of the summer working with Dave McKenna. Well he pulled me down from the ceiling, my head was stuck in it, my ship rose to the surface and sailed off. And I spent the better part of four years working with Dave. Everybody else was down at Berklee, and I was a little old for that anyhow. They were down there playing modal and learning scales and stuff. I was learning tunes like “Ship Without a Sail” and all this stuff and Dave just — he never called a tune, he never gave a tempo, he didn’t do anything, he just sat there and started playing. And you were either on board or you weren’t. And it was just night after night after night for one year. We started in May and finished on New Year’s Eve. That was the summer season. And one night we played duo — I can remember one night we played duo in the room on like a Wednesday night, a cold, rainy, late October night, for about thirteen people sat in the lounge. And they stayed from the first note to the last and you could hear the ice cubes melt. And it was so intense. And this went on just night after night, just tunes and I really © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

was a sponge at this point. I was really trying to soak up everything I could. And I was living in New York at the time. I had a $150 a month apartment and I’d just go in on June first and lock the door and turn off the electricity and come back in January or whatever. And I was also working with Marian McPartland at that time. So I was juggling a fairly serious calendar. And that was a wonderful gig for me. Because I had that gig when I moved to New York. So instead of coming to New York looking for a job I came to New York working with Marian with her trio.
